articles.title_orig: Warner Bros Gloom Sets In At Studio Amid Paramount Merger
articles.title_zh: Warner Bros Gloom Sets In At Studio Amid Paramount Merger
articles.content_orig:
Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
UPDATED: A Zoom call on Wednesday with 500 senior Warner Bros staffers to discuss Paramount ‘s settlement of the antitrust lawsuit brought by state attorneys general related to its merger with WBD did little to dissipate the gloomy, Mordor-like clouds over the Burbank lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.
The video call, which has been routine since Paramount won the $110 billion bid for Warner Bros Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration; Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar; WBD Chief Comms Officer Robert Gibbs; and HR boss Amy Girdwood . According to sources, the four conceded they didn’t have much visibility into Paramount’s plans for a newly combined company, but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison ‘s two-week timeframe he provided Monday.
The name and the leadership structure of the new company will likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that might be. We heard that Girdwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.
“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.
To say staffers were surprised by the AG settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.
“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the roller coaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”
Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. Ellison’s takeover of the cinematic institution founded by Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.
Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600 million from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.
The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, which don’t necessarily translate into job cuts, but rather by reducing inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e., real estate portfolios, data servers).
But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.
“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros over the past decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped WarnerMedia into the hands of Discovery.
Myriad people inside Warner Bros are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a post-merger windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the acquisition, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year: No one WB title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office, with the highest-grossing movie stateside being Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking; with its $186M net production cost and a global box office gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe DC Studios chose the wrong comic book character to adapt.
On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros marriage comes together is Digger, the $125M political satire starring Tom Cruise, directed by Alejandro G. Iñárritu and produced by Legendary. It opens on October 2. While domestic debut prospects are at around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like it did on One Battle After Another, as the four-time Oscar-winning filmmaker’s Doctor Strangelove -like epic is being primed as an awards-season contender. It is a chip Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.
The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion-dollar-grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot with Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on December 18. To date, the Denis Villeneuve franchise counts $1.12B at the global box office and eight Oscars.
We’ve heard on the Paramount side that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution. Warner Bros international distribution has more of a solid presence in offshore territory offices and staffers than Paramount, which needs to untangle itself from UIP. Paramount could find great muscle in Warners International distribution and marketing infrastructure.
While we were told by Paramount sources that the plan isn’t to create two studios, it might be wise for Ellison to keep each respective marketing team at their respective labels if he wants each studio working to the top of their creative merits and box office strengths: former Warner Bros exec Josh Goldstine presiding over global marketing and distribution at Paramount, and the team he built at Warners — Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing along with Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford–exactly over at Warners. Marketing and distribution rolls up and reports into the motion picture heads. During Warner Bros’ $4.38B grossing 2025, the trio of Nussbaum, Davin, and Stanford achieved great innovative marketing efficiencies, we’re told, and yes, those 11 Oscars for the Burbank, CA lot.
There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels-led Global Networks spinoff.
Yes, Warner Bros staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs: Former EVP Comms Katie Martin Kelly, prized by Warner Bros Motion Picture group co-heads Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, high-tailed it for Netflix as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue for poaching.
The merger closing will likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction, no longer bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.
“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”
And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.
What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros brand.”
Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”
For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros theatrical releases on the calendar dated between October 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a currently combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros, the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum; assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during merger talk time, and that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.
Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit due to ongoing talks with top-tier talent including director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business for the new Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.

articles.title_orig: What's really true in 'Brothers'? McConaughey, Harrelson set record straight
articles.title_zh: What's really true in 'Brothers'? McConaughey, Harrelson set record straight
articles.content_orig:
When Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey play exaggerated versions of their very famous selves in “Brothers” – right down to lookalike TV spouses, a potential McConaughey governor's run and a 30-year friendship – there’s one obvious question: How much of the Apple TV comedy series (first two episodes now streaming) is actually real?
Speaking to McConaughey, 56, and a noticeably shoeless, perpetually grinning Harrelson, 65, USA TODAY asked the longtime friends to lay a truth percentage on “Brothers.”
“65%,” McConaughey says immediately, surprising Harrelson.
“Really? I’d go lower,” Harrelson says, settling on a 36 percent truth percentage. "It’s based on us. But all the stories and characters are different.”
“Maybe I have a different definition of ‘based,’” McConaughey adds. “Maybe I give ‘based’ with a capital B in bold letters, and you give it lofty, lowercase cursive.”
Whatever anyone's definition of "based," “Brothers” takes its biggest swing at truth from the persistent, bizarrely plausible rumor that the two might actually be biological brothers. Each episode begins with the cheeky disclaimer, "Based on a true rumor." It’s a legit rumor born from the two families’ intertwined histories.
McConaughey’s own mother, Kay "Ma Mac" McConaughey, fueled the possibility when she suggested that she “knew” Harrelson’s absentee father, Charles Harrelson, during a period when McConaughey’s parents were separated – raising the holy-cow possibility that Charles Harrelson could be McConaughey’s biological father. The timeline fits.
Harrelson, who says he's willing to "cross swords" with McConaughey in some sort of joint urine-based DNA test, says McConaughey prefers to keep his head and zipper up, while moving on.
"I think it's BS," McConaughey explains of the brother linkage.
"That's 100 percent true," Harrelson says. "He wants to think it's BS, but he doesn't think it's BS. His mom and my dad did the horizontal bebop and they created this specimen right here."
McConaughey insists he just doesn't want to take the test to protect Harrelson's feeling.
"Because if it's not true, my buddy here is gonna be upset," McConaughey says. "I don't want that to happen."
In "Brothers," Harrelson and his family live in a technicolor bus on the McConaughey’s property – an exact replica of the biodiesel-powered “Mothership” former Chicago transit bus that Harrelson drove.
"The bus is real, or at least it's a one-to-one approximation," showrunner Lee Eisenberg says. "But we were not making a documentary here."
The families are in the ballpark, too. Harrelson has three daughters with his wife, Laura Louie. In “Brothers,” Brittany Ishibashi plays his wife, Joy, with Highdee Kuan and Oona Yaffe playing the couple's daughters, Olive and Kai.
McConaughey has three children with his real wife, Camila Alves. His “Brothers” family mirrors that setup, with Natalie Martinez playing wife Valentina and Nolan Almeida, Ella Grace Helton and Noah Carganilla playing their three children, Wyatt, Clara and River.
The real children are wildly different, admits Almeida, 18, who plays an adorably awkward version of McConaughey's 18-year-old actor son Levi.
"The show teeters between real-life and fiction, but my character is entirely fictional," Almeida says. "Levi has swagger. He's cool, like his father. My character Wyatt is not that at all."
Ma Mac is played by an outrageously fake-tanned Holland Taylor, the Emmy-winning star of "Two and a Half Men," who stirs up heightened TV trouble between the two longtime friends.
A major point in the truth column is the friendship and chaotic energy between the screen version of McConaughey and Harrelson and the real-life versions. The two "True Detective" stars stir up laughs and mishaps everywhere they go, including a seemingly routine trophy presentation at the Sept. 14 Emmy Awards.
The two joked onstage for an extended time onstage before the final award for best comedy series.
"They told us that they were under!" McConaughey insists about the Emmy producers. "They said, we've never said this before, but please stretch it out."
After finally giving the award to "Widow's Bay," a red shirt-wearing Harrelson neglected to exit the stage, and stood amid celebrating cast and crew, trapped but smiling during the acceptance speech.
"It would have been awkward just to walk away," Harrelson says. "So I just kind of embraced it."
"There's the genius of Woody Harrelson right there," McConaughey says.
The duo insist there's no more secrets on which to base a "Brothers" Season 2, which hasn't been discussed, partially pending the show's performance on Apple TV.
"Talking about Season 2 is kind of like writing your acceptance speech before you've won the award," says McConaughey.
"You know I had an acceptance speech in my pocket at the Emmys," adds Harrelson. "I never did get a chance to read that."

articles.title_orig: Maine Dems hammer Collins over report of pay-to-play probe. GOP senator calls it 'completely false'
articles.title_zh: Maine Dems hammer Collins over report of pay-to-play probe. GOP senator calls it 'completely false'
articles.content_orig:
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In the final weeks of 2019, a top fundraiser for Sen. Susan Collins walked into a perilous meeting at a Corner Bakery in Washington, D.C.
For the first time in her two-decade Senate career, the Republican lawmaker from Maine was in danger of losing her seat. President Donald Trump’s dismal approval ratings were dragging her down in the polls, and she was falling behind her likely 2020 Democratic challenger in fundraising.
Scott Reed, head of the Collins super PAC, was on a mission to close that gap. Reed was meeting that day with three executives from a Hawaiian defense contractor, Navatek. A year earlier, Collins had helped their company land a multimillion-dollar Navy research contract in Maine. Now, seated at a coffee shop not far from the U.S. Capitol, Reed asked them for a $500,000 donation.
Government contractors are banned from making political contributions. More consequentially, for the company to offer donations to Collins in exchange for an official action, or for Collins to accept, would constitute criminal bribery.
But the company did have such a proposal: Navatek was hungry for more government contracts in Maine. If they cut a big check, the CEO told Reed, Navatek wanted Collins to guarantee tens of millions of dollars in additional federal funding.
To skirt campaign finance laws and conceal the source of the funds, Navatek planned to funnel the donation through a shell company. The CEO wanted assurance that Collins would know where the money came from. Reed confirmed that she would, the executive said — and that Navatek would get its government contracts.
After the Corner Bakery meeting, Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, sent an initial $150,000 to the Collins super PAC using the shell company. Two months later, he told Navatek executives that Collins committed to getting the company $32 million in naval contracts, according to an internal company email reviewed by ProPublica.
Three years later, Kao holed up in a conference room to recount the Corner Bakery meeting to a group of four FBI agents and federal prosecutors. The FBI had seen through his shell company ruse, and in 2022 a grand jury indicted him for making illegal campaign contributions. No one working for Collins was charged.
Facing years in prison, Kao hoped to do less time by revealing the entire scheme.
What he told them has never before become public. The Corner Bakery meeting, he asserted, was just one episode in a sprawling pay-to-play operation that embroiled some of the most powerful figures in Congress.
Over three days at the U.S. attorney’s office in Honolulu, Kao laid out in devastating detail how his operation worked. He gave agents a 50-page document naming dozens of lobbyists, congressional staffers and members of Congress who he said helped him trade cash for contracts. Kao and his close associates had donated nearly $900,000 to dozens of politicians, allowing Navatek to establish operations in half a dozen states with over $40 million a year in government funding.
We’re still reporting on pay-for-play arrangements between powerful companies and elected officials.
I want to hear from you. Please feel free to send tips or story ideas. The best way to reach me is on Signal at 804-295-7201.
Most damningly, Kao told FBI agents and prosecutors, the company’s work for the government was of no real value. Navatek’s research under his stewardship never resulted in products the military wanted to buy, ProPublica found.
Kao’s tell-all interviews with the FBI lasted into late 2024. His confessions opened up an entirely new phase of the investigation. Agents sifted through hundreds of thousands of records seized during Kao’s arrest and found that many were consistent with his account of widespread influence peddling.
Kao had credibility issues. He was now a felon trying to avoid a lengthy prison sentence. And there were other challenges. Building a corruption case against elected officials requires extraordinary proof of a quid pro quo arrangement, in part because the Supreme Court has narrowed what counts as bribery.
Even so, by the end of 2024, the agents had enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers of both political parties. They asked their supervisors to approve a new investigation and contemplated using undercover operatives to gather more evidence. Although their effort was in its early stages, and it was unclear where it would lead, FBI agents asked Kao extensive questions about his dealings with Collins and her office.
Then Trump returned to the White House. Consumed by a campaign of vengeance , he stacked the Department of Justice with his personal lawyers and demanded a purge of anyone who had ever investigated him.
The specialized FBI and DOJ teams handling public corruption investigations, some of which were involved in Trump-related cases, were eviscerated. One of the agents who had taken Kao’s confession was pushed out as retribution for her role in investigating Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election. Dozens of agents and prosecutors quit amid the department’s destruction, including the career attorney assigned to Kao’s case.
Trump’s Justice Department no longer takes on public corruption in any meaningful fashion , former officials said. The investigation sparked by Kao’s revelations is dead. And the government is no longer talking to an informant who had offered a road map to corruption in Congress.
The White House referred ProPublica to the FBI.
FBI spokesperson Ben Williamson said the agency had investigated claims against Collins years ago “and ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign. Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.” Williamson said the Trump administration has removed agents only “if they have been found to have acted unethically, undermined the mission, or engaged in weaponization of law enforcement.”
Williamson did not respond to questions about the new investigation launched in 2024 based on Kao’s previously unreported cooperation with the FBI.
ProPublica is revealing the existence of the case for the first time. We reviewed a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI and thousands of pages of legal records, and interviewed dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations, and the FBI inquiry to conduct our own investigation. We independently corroborated much of Kao’s account. Whether or not Kao’s dealings with politicians amount to criminal bribery, the Trump Justice Department has little interest in finding out, and his sheer success reveals how easily influence is purchased in Washington today. This is the first in a series of stories drawn from our reporting.
Of all the politicians Navatek courted under Kao’s leadership, Collins was its most important patron. The senator’s office steered government contracts worth millions toward the company while her campaign was pumping Kao and his network for donations, according to emails seen by ProPublica. Sometimes they cut checks within 24 hours of the annual defense spending bill, which funds military contracts, clearing a key Senate hurdle.
Collins’ office did not specifically address questions about the Corner Bakery meeting, the senator’s relationship with Kao and the millions she helped appropriate for Navatek.
Annie Clark, Collins’ deputy chief of staff, told ProPublica in an email that Collins’ office “vigorously” denies allegations of bribery and pay-for-play made by Kao, calling his claims “outlandish.” Collins’ campaign was not part of the discussions between Kao and the super PAC, and her office “fully cooperated” with the FBI investigation, Clark said.

articles.title_orig: Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski: Idaho cold case leads detectives to 1982 Tylenol murders with cyanide in Chicago-area
articles.title_zh: Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski: Idaho cold case leads detectives to 1982 Tylenol murders with cyanide in Chicago-area
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO (WLS) -- Idaho investigators have identified a man they believe merits further scrutiny in the 1982 Tylenol murders, while acknowledging they have no evidence placing him in the Chicago area when the poisonings occurred.
The Ada County Sheriff's Office on Wednesday identified the man as Dr. Matthew Betkouski, a chemist known as the "Unknown Wanderer."
Betkouski, who had a history of mental illness, was found dead by suicide inside a Catholic church in Boise, Idaho, in December 1982. Investigators said their review uncovered comments he allegedly made to co-workers at different points in his career that drew their attention decades later.
Years before the Tylenol killings, Betkouski worked for a fragrance company in Jacksonville.
"Co-workers reported Dr. Betkouski discussing the perfect crime. And how cyanide could be used as a less messy way of taking one's life," Ada County Sheriff's Detective Tim Cooper said.
Investigators said Betkouski later made another similar comment while employed at Lockheed Martin in New Mexico in early 1982.
"Before he was terminated Dr. Betkouski made a comment about how poison could be introduced into over-the-counter capsules if a person wished to do so," Cooper said.
The announcement comes more than four decades after seven people died across the Chicago area after taking cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules. The victims included a 12-year-old child and three members of a single family in Arlington Heights. The deaths prompted the recall and destruction of millions of bottles of Tylenol.
Although James Lewis was later imprisoned on an extortion charge related to the case, authorities never identified him as the person who carried out the killings.
Ada County officials said investigators were able to place Betkouski in Chicago in late 1981, but found no evidence showing he was in the area when the poisonings occurred in September 1982.
"I cannot put his shoes in a pharmacy store aisle 44 years ago. But I also can't dismiss his statements, his actions," Cooper said.
WATCH: I-Team Investigates: The Tylenol Murders
The Chicago Police Department and Arlington Heights Police Department confirmed they have received the investigative file from Ada County and are reviewing the information. Neither agency provided additional details.
The FBI, however, cautioned against drawing conclusions from information that has not been substantiated.
In a statement, the bureau said: "There have been repeated claims over the past 44 years about alleged links to the Tylenol Murders which remain unsubstantiated. Out of respect for the ongoing, legitimate investigation, those impacted by the tragedy, and the law enforcement partners who have provided genuine support since the start, the FBI remains the lead on investigating and releasing credible information to the public once the evidence yields a true case resolution."
Michelle Rosen, whose mother, Mary Reiner, was among those killed in the poisonings, called for transparency and for investigative records to be made public.
"The Unknown Wanderer is not a random name pulled from thin air. He presents as a serious and compelling person of interest whose background merits careful examination," Rosen said in a statement.
The Tylenol murders changed how medications are packaged and are the reason behind the tamper proof bottles we have today.

Tune in for Craig Carton's unfiltered breakdown of how the Giants botched the injury narrative and where the franchise goes from here.
When New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a season-ending knee injury this week, we knew there'd be two reactions from the overwhelmingly liberal sports media.
First, they'd call for the Giants to sign Colin Kaepernick . They do it whenever an NFL team loses a quarterback, even though Kaepernick has not played professional football in a decade.
Second, they'd mock Dart’s injury because he made headlines in May by introducing President Donald Trump at a New York City event.
Both reactions materialized almost immediately.

Sports blogger Mike Florio was the first to urge the Giants to sign Kaepernick . Elsewhere, the usual suspects framed Dart's injury as political karma.
"Media types say 'Trump Curse' has struck again," wrote HuffPost in an article referring to Dart as a "Trump admirer."

Film and TV critic John Rocha shared a photo of Trump and Dart’s interaction, writing, " Everything he touches, y'all . Everything he touches..."

Other outlets adopted a similar tone.
"Jaxson Dart's injury reignites Trump sports curse possibility," joked USA Today.
The people making these jokes will insist they are harmless. Perhaps some of them believe that. But they know exactly what they are doing and how their majority anti-Trump audiences will respond.
Look at the comments under The Athletic’s report about Dart’s season-ending injury. The comment section resembles a fringe political message board, with readers celebrating the injury, asking whether Dart is "vaxxed" and claiming that he deserves this because he supported Trump.
Interestingly, we do not know whether Dart is a Trump supporter.
Yes, he introduced Trump at an event. But introducing the sitting president is not, on its face, a political statement. The event also took place in the city where Dart plays quarterback. For all we know, Dart would have accepted the same opportunity if a Democrat were in the White House.
Despite what the legacy media tells you, some Americans would welcome the chance to associate with the president regardless of their political views. In fact, we suspect most Americans fall into that category.

That said, we can probably deduce that Dart doesn't consider Trump a Nazi . And that is enough for some in the media to call him "MAGA" and poke fun at his injury.
In 2020, then-ESPN commentator Mark Jones shared posts mocking 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa after Bosa suffered a serious knee injury. The posts referred to Bosa as "MAGA Bosa" and said he deserved to suffer the injury because he stood during the national anthem.
Three years later, former ESPN host Keith Olbermann celebrated when Aaron Rodgers tore his Achilles in the opening minutes of the Jets’ season.
"Another #SuddenLisfranc due to failure to vaccinate," Olbermann posted on X.
When the Jets wrote that Rodgers’ injury was "Not the way any of us wanted it to go," Olbermann responded: "Define 'any.'"
This type of behavior reflects how many Americans suffering from Trump Derangement Syndrome (TDS) react when something awful happens to a Trump voter or someone who does not express open disdain for the president. They genuinely believe that anyone who does not hate Trump as deeply as they do is unworthy and deserves to be punished.
Sticking to sports commentators, Jemele Hill immediately denounced Charlie Kirk as a racist days after his murder.
Of course, sports injuries are not as serious as death. But they matter. Professional athletes have short careers. Major injuries can derail them, and the consequences are not merely physical. Serious injuries can also take a mental toll.
And yet liberal sports fans and media figures abandon common decency whenever an injury allows them to score cheap political points.

articles.title_orig: Qualcomm’s New Minuscule Sound Chip Fits Wi-Fi Lossless Audio in Your Ears
articles.title_zh: Qualcomm’s New Minuscule Sound Chip Fits Wi-Fi Lossless Audio in Your Ears
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
LAHAINA, Hawaii—AI is everywhere at Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit, including the actual air! Sort of. The company had a number of AI technology demos on hand, and the one that caught my ear involved silence.
We're all familiar with how noise-cancelling headphones work. They use embedded mics to capture ambient sound, then process it with algorithms to generate an inverse sound wave that cancels it out. They function the same way whether you're listening to music or making phone calls. In the latter case, the headphones use the inverse wave to cancel out the surrounding din so you and your caller don't hear it. The result depends somewhat on the strength of the manufacturer's algorithms; some are better at it than others.
But what if you didn't need noise-cancelling earphones for crystal-clear calls at all? Phones already use the onboard mics to process and lower background noise; they've done so for many years. What I saw takes things to a whole new level.
Qualcomm had a test device on-site with its new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor. As described to me, the phone could triangulate its mics to create an algorithmically defined sound bubble around it, silencing everything outside it.
The invisible bubble had a radius of about 5 feet for the purposes of the demonstration, but it can be made any size you want or need. A Qualcomm staffer made a call with the device and played sound from a nearby Bluetooth speaker, about 10 feet away. Despite the noise, his phone captured and transmitted only his voice; it completely stripped the Bluetooth speaker's sound from his call, making it inaudible on the other end of the line. The algorithms were also trained to silence extraneous noise from inside the bubble. The staffer started clapping right next to the phone while he was speaking, and still, the only sound that came through the other phone was his voice.
This could be a great tool not just for call quality, but for privacy. Consider how many times you've had to take a call in a space where it wasn't appropriate for your caller to hear the background noise, such as certain work environments. Or times when you didn't have a pair of headphones handy. There's definite potential here.
Qualcomm didn't say if or when this type of technology would reach actual shipping devices, but it's a neat use of AI to accomplish something helpful for a basic activity like making phone calls.
To think about it in a much cooler way: Qualcomm used AI to create a force field that blocks sound. How rad is that?
I’m PCMag’s Managing Editor for Consumer Electronics content, overseeing an experienced team of reviewers and product testers. I’ve been covering technology for more than 25 years. Prior to PCMag, I worked at outlets such as Android Authority, Fortune, InformationWeek, and Phonescoop.

BEIJING—China's Commerce Ministry confirmed Thursday that its senior trade negotiators had held their first talks with the U.S. on artificial intelligence.
Spokesperson He Yadong told reporters the two sides also discussed plans for reducing tariffs, and extending trade arrangements agreed in Kuala Lumpur last October.
He was referring to China's Vice Premier He Lifeng meeting with his counterpart, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in New York in the runup to the summit this week between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As Xi landed in the U.S., Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday the two countries agreed to extend a trade truce to January. The truce, reached in October 2025, kept tariffs lower and limited China's export controls on rare earths, which are critical components of semiconductors and many household goods, as well as defense products.
Earlier in the week, Bessent said the two sides discussed establishing an AI dialogue and a mechanism to alert each other about AI risks.
The Chinese confirmation of the AI talks came just hours before Xi and Trump were scheduled to begin talks in Washington, D.C., as part of a state visit.
Trump said in a Truth Social post early Thursday that the leaders would discuss AI.
"A big day with President Xi of China. Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!" he wrote.
The president has been vocal about his opposition to further regulation of AI and reiterated his position to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that: "We're going to encourage it, not rein it in."
The ministry added the two sides held constructive, candid talks, and reached multiple points of consensus.
Both countries are weighing how to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology after recent incidents involving AI systems raised fears that increasingly autonomous models could make attacks faster and harder to contain.

articles.content_orig:
China’s Xi visits US as Trump bets on stabilising global relations
United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.
Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.
Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.
At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.
In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.
Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing , whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.
Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.
His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry , a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI , and US ties to Taiwan , the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese ‌Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could ⁠do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series ⁠of smaller things”.
“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.
The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.
“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.
Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.
On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.
She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.
“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

Jonathan Schanzer, the executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, previews Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House Thursday against the backdrop of the U.S.-Iran war.
President Donald Trump needs to warn Chinese President Xi Jinping against pursuing a "dangerous alliance" with Iran when the two world leaders meet at the White House Thursday, an expert told Fox News Digital.
Jonathan Schanzer, the executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, made the remark after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi reportedly told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during talks in Beijing last week that China was prepared to play a "constructive role" in resolving international disputes. The U.S. war against Iran is nearing the 7-month mark.
"The president needs to tell Xi Jinping that this is a dangerous alliance. The Chinese assistance to the Iranian regime has actually spanned a number of fronts," Schanzer told Fox News Digital. "The first is, of course, the provision of drone parts and motors. This has actually helped the Islamic Republic attack all of its neighbors.
"On top of that, they've been providing some dual-use chemicals that have been helping the Iranians with their missile program. On top of that, we've watched a lot of targeting that looks a little bit too precise for the Iranian regime. So that looks like it may be helped from the Chinese as well," Schanzer continued.
CHINA'S XI JINPING SET TO ARRIVE IN WASHINGTON FOR HIGH-STAKES TRUMP SUMMIT AS AI SUPREMACY BATTLE LOOMS LARGE
President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping participate in an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Alex Brandon/AP)
"On top of that, there's an economic relationship that I think is keeping the Islamic Republic afloat while it continues to hammer away at the oil economy worldwide. These are all things that need to stop. And the hope here is, of course, that Donald Trump is going to make a demand here that Xi Jinping stop all of this," he said.
When asked to respond to the Chinese and Iranian foreign ministers meeting in Beijing, Schanzer said, "When you look at what's happening here, it's pretty clear that the Chinese government is just not ashamed of this at all."
TRUMP TO ASK XI TO FREE WRONGFULLY DETAINED US CITIZEN AS WIFE SPEAKS OUT
Flags are marched in as an Air China airplane carrying Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan arrives at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)
"In other words, there's a war going on. The Iranians have spiked the price of oil. They have clogged the Strait of Hormuz. They're looking to do the same in the Bab al-Mandab, and they are completely unashamed by this. It's important for Donald Trump to bare his teeth here and to make it clear that the Iranians cannot get this kind of support and that the Chinese government is at risk of escalating with the United States," he added.
A senior administration official told Fox News Digital that when Trump last visited China in mid-May, he and Xi agreed that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon and that the Strait of Hormuz should be reopened without any tolls.

"I think the big thing in the background here is that we're obviously watching great power competition between two of the world's largest economies and largest militaries," Schanzer also said ahead of Thursday’s meeting. "The thing that I watch right now is that Taiwan is clearly the main target for the Chinese Communist Party. They want to reunite with the island, as they would call it, and they're putting enormous pressure on Taiwan with that in mind. The United States needs to stand pat here. We have an enormous amount invested in chips in Taiwan, the Taiwan Semiconductor Company. This is the big one here. And if we're going to win the AI race, we need to maintain control of that company. More importantly, we need to make sure that that island remains secure."
